subject: biology

moments.title: Scheele and Priestley discover oxygen
moments.who: Carl Wilhelm Scheele (Sweden) and Joseph Priestley (England) — independently
moments.body:
Scheele isolates 'fire air' (oxygen) around 1772 by heating various metal oxides. His findings are published in 1777, delayed by his publisher.

Priestley independently isolates the same gas in 1774 by focusing sunlight onto mercuric oxide. He notes that a candle burns more brightly in it and a mouse can live longer. He calls it 'dephlogisticated air' — fitting his (incorrect) phlogiston theory.
moments.takeaway: A new gas is isolated. Both discoverers interpret it within frameworks soon to be discarded.

moments.title: Lavoisier explains combustion as oxidation
moments.body:
Priestley meets Lavoisier in Paris in 1774 and tells him of the gas. Lavoisier names it 'oxygène' (acid-former), proposes that combustion is union of substances with oxygen (not loss of 'phlogiston'), and overturns the phlogiston theory.

Lavoisier shows that respiration is essentially slow combustion — animals breathe in oxygen, breathe out CO2, and the same proportions hold as for burning charcoal. His quantitative experiments inaugurate modern chemistry.

quote.text: Respiration is therefore a combustion, very slow it is true, but otherwise perfectly similar to that of charcoal.

moments.takeaway: Animal respiration is chemistry. Burning food in the body explains body heat and waste gases.

moments.title: Lavoisier executed
moments.who: Lavoisier, Place de la Révolution, Paris
moments.body:
Lavoisier, as a former tax farmer under the ancien régime, is guillotined during the Terror. The judge reportedly says 'The Republic has no need of scientists.' His friend Lagrange laments: 'It took them only an instant to cut off his head, but France may not produce another such head in a century.'

Lavoisier is 50. His widow, Marie-Anne Paulze (a chemist herself, who illustrated his books and translated chemical texts), preserves his papers.
moments.takeaway: Founding modern chemistry doesn't protect you from politics.

moments.title: Liebig and animal chemistry
moments.body:
Liebig extends Lavoisier's view: foods can be classified by what they're oxidised to. Carbohydrates and fats are 'respiratory' (oxidised for heat). Proteins are 'plastic' (build tissue, sometimes oxidised for energy too).

Liebig also (incorrectly) believes plant carbon comes from soil humus — wrong, but his fertilizer chemistry transforms agriculture.
moments.takeaway: Food chemistry begins. Macronutrients are classified by metabolic fate.

moments.title: Krebs cycle
moments.body:
Hans Krebs, having fled Nazi Germany, works out the cycle of reactions by which acetyl groups are oxidised to CO2 with the reduction of NAD+ to NADH. The reactions are eight; the substrate (citrate) lends its name.

The cycle takes place in mitochondria. Together with electron transport, it represents the bulk of aerobic ATP production. Krebs wins the 1953 Nobel Prize.
moments.takeaway: The chemistry of cellular respiration is mapped reaction by reaction. Lavoisier's 'slow combustion' is now an enzymatic cycle.

now.title: Respiration today
now.body:
Aerobic respiration is mapped from glucose to ATP at atomic resolution. Mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in many diseases. We can measure cellular oxygen consumption in real time (Seahorse extracellular flux analysers) to phenotype metabolism.

Applications: mitochondrial medicine, exercise physiology, sports science, aging research, drug screening.
now.open_questions: What aspect of mitochondrial decline causes aging? Can we therapeutically boost mitochondrial biogenesis? Why are some mutations in oxidative phosphorylation genes tolerated while others are lethal? How does metabolic flexibility (switching between fuels) work mechanistically?

reflection: Lavoisier was executed for being a tax collector. Priestley fled to America after Birmingham mobs burned down his lab for his support of the French Revolution. Krebs fled Germany. Buchner died at the Eastern Front. The biochemistry of respiration was developed by people whose lives were constantly disrupted by political and military violence. What does science achieve in spite of, and what does it lose to, history?
